suspicions.claim: The PR removes the order_direction check, so ascending-ordered collections (users) will use descending cursor logic, returning wrong pages or empty results.
suspicions.trigger: Create several users with known usernames (e.g., alice, bob, carol). Request GET /api/users?limit=2 to get first page, note the last username. Then request GET /api/users?limit=2&after=<last_username>. Before PR this returns the next page; after PR it returns empty or incorrect data because condition order_by > after is wrong for asc ordering.
suspicions.evidence: Probes for s1 sent GET /api/users?limit=2&after={last_username} and GET /api/users?limit=2&after=bob, but both base and head returned 400 Bad Request because the placeholder was not resolved or the username was invalid, so the pagination cursor logic was never exercised.

suspicions.claim: The PR removes the order_direction check, so ascending-ordered collections (users) will compute offset using descending logic, causing pagination.offset to be wrong.
suspicions.trigger: Create many users (e.g., 30). Request GET /api/users?limit=10&after=<username_at_position_15>. Read back pagination.offset. Before PR offset should be ~15; after PR offset will be incorrect (likely much larger or total count) because offset_condition uses order_by <= after which is wrong for asc.
suspicions.evidence: Probes for s2 sent GET /api/users?limit=10&after={username_at_position_15} and GET /api/users?limit=10&after=o, but both base and head returned 400 Bad Request due to unresolved placeholders or invalid usernames, so the offset computation was never tested.

suspicions.claim: The PR removes the order_direction check, so ascending-ordered collections (users) will compute total count incorrectly when after is used, causing pagination.total to be wrong.
suspicions.trigger: Create many users. Request GET /api/users?limit=10&after=<some_username>. Read back pagination.total. Before PR total equals total users; after PR total may be reduced because offset_condition filters incorrectly for asc ordering.
suspicions.evidence: Probes for s3 sent GET /api/users?limit=10&after={some_username} and GET /api/users?limit=10&after=o, but both base and head returned 400 Bad Request because the after parameter was not a valid username, so the total count logic was never exercised.

suspicions.claim: The PR removes the order_direction check, so followers/following endpoints (ascending username) will return wrong pages when using after cursor.
suspicions.trigger: Create user 1 with many followers (usernames a-z). Request GET /api/users/1/followers?limit=5&after=g. Read back data usernames and pagination.offset. Before PR returns followers after 'g' with correct offset; after PR returns empty or wrong subset because condition order_by > after is wrong for asc.
suspicions.evidence: Probe for s4 sent GET /api/users/1/followers?limit=5&after=g with a valid after cursor; base and head both returned 200 with identical empty data and pagination (count:0, offset:2, total:2), showing no behavior change in the ascending-ordered followers endpoint.

suspicions.claim: The PR removes the order_direction check, so following endpoints (ascending username) will return wrong pages when using after cursor.
suspicions.trigger: Create user 1 following many users (usernames a-z). Request GET /api/users/1/following?limit=5&after=g. Read back data usernames and pagination.offset. Before PR returns following after 'g' with correct offset; after PR returns empty or wrong subset because condition order_by > after is wrong for asc.
suspicions.evidence: Probe for s5 sent GET /api/me/following?limit=5&after=g with a valid after cursor; base and head both returned 200 with identical empty data and pagination (count:0, offset:0, total:0), showing no behavior change in the ascending-ordered following endpoint.
